# Treasury Cash Flow Forecasting 

## AI-Powered Forecasting System for Aperam

---

# 1\. Executive Summary

This project aims to develop an AI-powered cash flow forecasting system for Aperam’s Treasury team. Aperam treasury manages €60M+ in weekly trade receivables and €50M+ in trade payables across European entities. Current manual forecasting from individual entities achieves \~90% Week 1 accuracy but declines to 64-83% by Week 4, with no visibility beyond 4 weeks and limits optimal liquidity decisions. 

![][image1]  
*Tab 1\. 2025 cash flow forecast accuracy metrics*

The primary objective is to improve forecast accuracy from the current 70-90% baseline to 80-95% across an 8-week horizon, with the goal of reducing borrowing costs by €XXM annually through more accurate cash flow predictions. The system will use machine learning models (XGBoost, LightGBM, LSTM etc.) to predict weekly cash flows for Trade Receivables (TRR) and Trade Payables (TRP) Reval liquidity groups. The approach emphasizes enhancing existing treasury processes rather than replacing them, with rigorous backtesting and a phased pilot implementation.

| Horizon | Current State | Target Accuracy | Value |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Weeks 1-2 | 88-92% | 90-95% | Modest improvement |
| Weeks 3-4 | 64-83% | 80-90% | 10-20% improvement |
| Weeks 5-8 | No forecast | 75-85% | **New capability** |

*Tab 2\. Success Metrics*  
Forecast accuracy will be measured using WAPE (primary) and MAE/RMSE (secondary) at weekly horizons (W1–W8). 

# 2\. Problem Statement & Business Context

## 2.1 Current Challenges

Treasury manages complex weekly cash flows across Europe with decisions about credit lines, investments and funding depending upon the forecasts. The treasury team currently achieves high accuracy in Week 1 forecasts (approximately 90%) but experiences significant accuracy degradation over longer horizons, dropping to 74% by Week 4\. This limits the treasury team's ability to:

* Optimize borrowing costs through better liquidity planning  
* Make informed decisions about excess cash investment  
* Arrange credit lines proactively rather than reactively  
* Manage working capital more efficiently across multiple entities and currencies

## 2.2 Business Objectives

* Extend forecast horizon from 4 weeks to 8 weeks with reliable accuracy  
* Reduce forecast error by 5-15 percentage points across all time horizons  
* Decrease borrowing costs by €XXM annually through improved cash visibility  
* Provide confidence intervals to quantify forecast uncertainty

## 2.3 Scope

| Included | 21 Aperam entities, Trade Receivables (TRR) \+ Trade Payables (TRP), 3 years daily data |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Excluded** | ELG & ASA divisions, other liquidity groups  |
| **Constraints** | Weekly forecasts, no external market data in V1 |

*Tab 3\. Scope of the Project*

## 3.4 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

The exploratory data analysis focused on two main data sources: the actuals dataset (625,320 rows of transaction data from Jan 2022 to Oct 2025\) and the liquidity plans dataset (31,666 rows of treasury forecasts). The ‘actuals’ data involved 18 entities after filtering for receivables and payables, with varying data completeness, with some entities like V756 (ASSS Italy) showing comprehensive historical coverage while others like 82J (ASSS USA) exhibit only 41 weeks of actuals data. An unexpected finding was 15,981 weekend transactions, confirmed as legitimate after consulting the treasury team. 

### 3.4.1 Entity Analysis

Entity analysis shows that only 15 of 18 filtered entities have the required min threshold 52 weeks of historical data for machine learning models, which need a full seasonal cycle. Three entities (82J, 20B2, 25A4) lack sufficient data due to pipeline issues, inconsistent input, or recent acquisition. These three will be excluded from model training, using their submitted liquidity plans as forecasts instead. This approach ensures full entity coverage while allowing for future inclusion in model training as more data becomes available.

| Category | Count | Data Coverage | Treatment |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Tier 1: Full ML Modeling | 15 | 52+ weeks | Ensemble Models (XGB, LGB, LSTM) |
| Tier 2: Pass-through | 3 (82J, 20B2, 25A4) | \< 52 weeks | Use treasury LP forecast; Reassess when more data is available |

*Tab 8\. Entity Split*

### 3.4.2 Liquidity Plan Characteristics

The liquidity plan dataset shows structural patterns that help with feature engineering and data preprocessing. Entities create rolling four-week forecasts, and these predictions reveal how forecast confidence changes over time. Not all entities provide a full four-week forecast, reflecting different forecasting practices. For missing forecasts, we will preserve as NaN as the tree based models would be able to handle those.  Additionally, entities have specific patterns, with some having only Trade Receivables and others Trade Payables. The modeling approach needs to consider these entity-specific behaviors through "entity profiling" instead of treating all entities the same.

## 3.5 Data Quality Governance

The project focuses on continuous data quality monitoring, moving beyond one-time discoveries from initial analysis. This involves systematic validation processes before each model retraining cycle, including checking data continuity, correct currency conversion, and entity data coverage. The process requires treasury review of any new anomalies before implementing automated corrections, preventing the removal of legitimate business information.

Documentation of all data quality decisions and entity treatment rules is a critical component. This ensures clarity for future teams on decisions like pass-through forecasting for certain entities, retaining weekend transactions, and currency conversion logic, preventing regressions and revisiting settled decisions. The decision log in this document, along with code comments and operational runbooks, will guide ongoing model maintenance.

# 4\. Solution Architecture

## 4.1 Core Philosophy

Our solution will enhance treasury expertise rather than replacing it. We integrate treasury liquidity plans as key inputs, leveraging human knowledge of upcoming events and operational changes alongside historical data patterns (seasonality, calendar effects, entity-specific behaviors). This combined approach should produce more accurate forecasts than either method alone. The system will be designed to be iterative, delivering value with current data while allowing for future enhancements as more data sources become available.

## 4.2 Feature Engineering

Our feature engineering will aim to balance complexity with data limitations (weekly aggregated transactions). We focus on temporal patterns, entity traits, calendar effects, and treasury forecasts (liquidity plans), \~ 100 features including lag variables, rolling statistics, calendar indicators, and trend measurements.

A key challenge is that simple weekly aggregation loses daily transaction pattern details (e.g., month-end spikes). To address this, we'll keep daily data during early feature engineering to extract sophisticated temporal features, then aggregate to weekly. These daily-to-weekly features capture insights like the percentage of transactions on month-end or daily amount variations, providing richer signals than simple weekly sums.

### 4.2.1 Core Feature Categories

Here are the core feature categories that will be used in the AI-powered cash flow forecasting system:

* **Lag Features:** These are crucial for time series forecasting, using past data to predict the future. We'll use 52 weekly lags (t-1 to t-52) to capture immediate, monthly, and annual patterns. This 52-week horizon dictates our minimum data requirement for entities.  
* **Rolling Statistics:** These summarize recent history to understand trends and volatility. We'll use 4-week and 12-week rolling averages to smooth noise and provide context, and 26-week rolling standard deviations to measure volatility. These features complement lag features, offering the model flexibility.  
* **Calendar Features:** These capture recurring temporal patterns like annual seasonality (week-of-year), monthly effects (payroll), and quarter-end impacts. These features apply broadly, independent of entity or historical patterns.  
* **Trend Features:** These measure whether cash flows are increasing, decreasing, or stable. Linear trend slopes over 12 weeks quantify momentum, and trend acceleration metrics signal inflection points. These are valuable for operational changes, helping the model detect shifts in patterns.  
* **Treasury liquidity plan forecasts** (Week 1-4) are incorporated as features. These capture expert expectations based on operational knowledge and events not in historical data. The model learns to weigh these projections based on their historical accuracy, trusting near-term forecasts more if they're reliable.  
* **Entity Encoding:** Entity-specific patterns are encoded using one-hot encoding for the 15 Tier 1 entities. This allows the model to learn unique base levels and seasonalities for each entity. Gradient boosting models automatically learn feature interactions (e.g., how treasury forecasts affect specific entities or how month-end impacts receivables vs. payables) through their tree structure, without manual engineering. Category encoding (Trade Receivables vs. Trade Payables) enables a single model to learn patterns across both, improving efficiency given the modest dataset size.

| Category | Count | Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Lag Features | 52 | t-1 through t-52 (one year lookback) |
| Rolling Statistics | \~18 | 4/12/26/52-week rolling mean, median, std, min, max, trend, and volatility |
| Calendar Features | \~12 | Week of the year, month-end, quarter-end flags |
| Daily Patterns | \~8 | count of transactions in the week, daily std dev |
| Trend Features | \~8 | acceleration metrics, momentum indicators |
| Liquidity Plans | 4 | LP\_W1, LP\_W2 |
| Entity Encoding | 16 | 15 entity one-hot \+ Liquidity group binary  |

*Tab 9\. Model Feature Categories*

## 4.3 Recursive Forecasting Strategy

The forecasting architecture uses a recursive prediction method, where a single model predicts one week ahead, and that prediction then informs the next week's forecast, continuing for the full 8-week horizon. This approach naturally will show declining accuracy over longer horizons due to error compounding, providing transparent insights into forecast uncertainty for better decision-making.  
![][image2]  
*Fig 1\. Recursive Forecasting Approach*

## 4.4 Multi-Model Ensemble Architecture

The solution will employ an ensemble of three model types: XGBoost, LightGBM, and LSTM neural networks. Gradient boosted decision trees (XGBoost and LightGBM) are excellent at identifying complex patterns and interactions within features, handling missing data, and providing interpretable insights. LSTM neural networks complement these by modeling temporal dependencies in cash flow data. We will add a final forecast that’s a simple average of the three models, which effectively prevents overfitting and provides robustness against individual model failures. 

### 4.4.1 Stack Ensemble Design

Out-of-fold predictions from individual models (LightGBM, XGB…) will feed a ridge-regression meta-learner, producing horizon specific weighted outputs. Dynamic per entity weighting will adjust model contributions based on recent rolling performance to stabilize tail errors. 

## 4.5 Production Architecture

The production system will operate on a weekly cadence, automatically extracting data from DENODO, retraining models, generating forecasts, and delivering outputs to treasury stakeholders.

### 4.5.1 Data Flow

* Source Layer: REVAL (core TMS) feeds daily transactions to SAS data warehouse  
* Data Infrastructure: SAS performs ETL to DENODO virtual data layer   
* ML Pipeline: Azure/AWS ML connects to DENODO weekly to extract fresh actuals and liquidity plans  
* Processing: Automated data quality validation → feature engineering → model training/inference  
* Output Delivery: Forecasts stored in central repository, could be exposed via Power BI dashboards and CSV exports

### 4.5.2 Key Components

| Component | Purpose | Frequency | Critical Features |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Data Extraction | Pull Actuals \+ LP from DENODO | Weekly (Tue noon) | Incremental load, retry logic |
| Quality Checks | Validate entities, gaps, currency etc | Per extraction | Auto-alerts on failures |
| Feature Engineering | Generate \~100 model features | Per training run | Preserve patterns |
| Model Training | Retrain models on latest data  | Weekly/On-demand | Time series CV, hyperparameter tuning |
| Model Registry | Version control | Continuous | Automatic rollback if accuracy declines beyond a threshold |
| Inference Pipeline | Generate Forecasts  | Weekly (post-training) | Recursive prediction, Confidence intervals |
| Monitoring | Track accuracy  | Continuous | Eg: Alert if Week1 accuracy \< 85% |
| BI Dashboard | Interactive forecast exploration | Real-time updates | Entity drill down, Accuracy trends |
| CSV/Raw File exports | Forecast output files  | Weekly |  |

*Tab 10\. Key Components of the System*

### 4.5.3 Monitoring & Alerts

* Data Quality Alert: Immediate notification if extraction fails or validation errors detected  
* Model Performance Alert: Daily email if Week 1 forecast accuracy drops below 85% threshold  
* Drift Alert: Weekly report flagging entities with degrading accuracy trends (\>15% decline over 4 weeks)

### 4.5.4 Fallback Strategy

* If model training fails: Use previous week's model for inference  
* If inference fails for specific entity: Use treasury's submitted LP as pass-through forecast  
* If complete system failure: Treasury reverts to manual process with XX-hour resolution SLA

## 4.6. Alternate Horizon Modeling

To mitigate error compounding, a direct multi-horizon modeling approach will be evaluated in parallel. Comparative back testing will determine whether recursive or direct models yield superior horizon stability and performance. 

## 4.7. Deployment Strategy

The deployment follows a 3-phase approach with strict go/no-go criteria at each gate, minimizing risk while enabling rapid feedback cycles. 

| Phase | Duration | Entities | Usage | Success Criteria |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Shadow mode | XX weeks | All 15 Tier 1 | View only | Forecasts generated successfully |
| Pilot | XX weeks | All 15 Tier 1 | Secondary validation | Meet Accuracy targets |
| Production Rollout | \- | All 15 Tier 1 \+ 3 Tier 2 | Primary decision input | Meet Accuracy targets |

*Tab 11\. Deployment Strategy*

# 5\. Success Metrics and Validation Framework

## 5.1 Accuracy Targets

Our project aims to significantly improve cash flow forecast accuracy over an extended 8-week horizon, surpassing current manual performance. Targets are set with the understanding that confidence naturally declines over longer periods.

* **Weeks 1-2:** We target 90-95% accuracy (WAPE), a modest but achievable improvement over the current 88-92% for Week 1, extending comparable quality to Week 2\.  
* **Weeks 3-4:** Targets range from 80-90% accuracy, a meaningful leap beyond the current 64-83% by Week 4\.   
* **Weeks 5-8:** We aim for \~75-85% accuracy, providing data-driven forecasts where none currently exist. Even at the lower end, this visibility should enable better long-term investment and facility planning.

## 5.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation

No single metric fully captures forecast quality, so we track five complementary metrics:

| Metric | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| WAPE | Primary metric. Weighted Absolute % Error \- emphasizes accuracy on large flows, robust to near-zero values |
| MAE | Mean Absolute Error in EUR \- shows typical error magnitude in business units |
| RMSE | Root Mean Squared Error \- penalizes large outlier errors that cause business problems |
| Directional | % correct positive/negative predictions \- critical for borrow vs invest decisions |
| MAPE | Mean Absolute % Error \- reported for large values only (can be unreliable with near-zero denominators) |

*Tab 11\. Model Evaluation Metrics*

All metrics are disaggregated by forecast week (1-8), liquidity category (Trade Receivables vs. Trade Payables), and entity tier (full ML vs. pass-through) for granular performance insights.

## 5.3 Validation Approach

Our validation strategy combines technical rigor with practical business insights:

* **Time Series Cross-Validation:** We use an expanding window approach, training on all historical data up to a cutoff and testing on the subsequent XX weeks. This mimics production deployment and critically ensures recursive forecasting is properly implemented, using predictions rather than actuals for future weeks.  
* **Business Validation and Pilot Testing:** This involves treasury workshops to review sample forecasts, assessing alignment with operational reality. A XX-week pilot will run model forecasts in parallel with manual liquidity plans, allowing the treasury team to build confidence, understand model behavior, and identify areas where the model might miss crucial context. Success is measured by the treasury team's willingness to use the forecasts for real decisions, supported by feature importance visualizations for explainability.

# 6\. Decision Log

Critical decisions made during EDA and planning phases, documenting rationale for future reference.

| Decision | Rationale |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Exclude entities with \<52 weeks actuals from ML training** | Need full annual cycle for seasonal pattern learning. Entities 82J, 20B2, 25A4 use pass-through until sufficient history. |
| **Retain weekend transactions (15,981 records)** | Treasury confirmed legitimate business activity. Weekly aggregation handles naturally. |
| **Preserve missing LP forecasts as NaN (don't impute)** | Incomplete forecast arrays reflect actual behavior, not data errors. Tree models handle natively. |
| **Fix currency conversion (use historical euroFX rates)** | Non-EUR plans had FX=1.0. Daily historical rates ensure true EUR conversion. |
| **Recursive 1-week forecasting**  | Mirrors production deployment, measures error compounding. Avoids train-test skew. |
| **Unified model with category feature (not separate TRR/TRP models)** | Pools information across categories, improves efficiency with modest dataset  |
| **Include treasury LP forecasts as model features** | Leverages domain knowledge about upcoming events. Model learns appropriate weighting.  |
| **Entity-liquidity group profiling**  | Treasury revealed some entities have either TRR or TRP. Profile these behaviors. (refer Appendix A) |

*Tab 12\. Decision Log*
